Effect of Layup on thermal stresses: Thermo-structural analyses on various layups were performed in an attempt to reduce transverse tensile stresses in tank due to internal pressure. Earlier structural analyses showed plenty of margin for stresses along the fiber direction, but in the transverse direction stresses were much closer to the allowable limit. To reduce transverse stresses, an effort was made to determine optimal layups for wound cylinders. The following layup from Farhood et. al. [4] i.e. [90/90/90/90/20/-20/……/-20/90/90/90/90] was chosen for an evaluation via structural analysis. The 90 degree ply refers to ply along the hoop direction. This layup reduced the transverse stresses in the tape relative to the layup analyzed in prior studies (i.e. +55/-55). This layup was further studied/analyzed by varying the angle of the non-hoop ply to 10 degrees, 20 degrees and 30 degrees i.e. [90/90/90/90/10/-10/……/10/-10/90/90/90/90] and [90/90/90/90/30/-30/……30/-30/90/90/90/90]. The resulting transverse stresses are shown in Figure 14. The contour plots show highest stresses in all the plies through the thickness. As can be seen, these stresses are far lower than the 42 MPa stress value seen in the default layup used in the first design [55/-55/+55/-55]. The lowest transverse stresses are for a ply angle of 10 degrees. However, this angle may present difficulties during manufacture and such considerations may force a change to higher tape angles e.g. 20 degrees or 30 degrees. As is known, micro- cracking contributes to the permeability of gases through the composite, and one source of micro-cracking is inter-laminar stresses. These are typically lower when the ply angles between adjacent plies are low. Furthermore, to reduce the propagation of micro-cracks from one ply to another, Bechel et. al. [5] suggested that having higher angles between adjacent plies is preferrable e.g. 0/90 rather than 0/45 is preferrable. This requirement stands in conflict with the prior requirement where a lower difference in ply angles are preferred to reduce thermal stresses. Hence further FE analyses are required to reconcile these requirements and optimize layup to minimize permeability.
